\section{Inference Efficiency}
\label{app:latency}

Table~\ref{tab:latency} reports inference throughput on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (96\,GB; batch size 1, sequence length 2048, fp16, averaged over 100 forward passes).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Inference latency on LLaMA-3.1-8B (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, batch=1, seq=2048, fp16, 100 forward passes). Overhead is relative to dense inference.}
\label{tab:latency}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Method & Sparsity & ms/fwd & tok/s & Overhead \\
\midrule
Dense & 0\% & 119.11$\pm$0.57 & 17{,}195 & --- \\
\midrule
KL predictor-only & 30\% & 126.64$\pm$0.70 & 16{,}172 & +6.3\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
KL predictor-only & 50\% & 126.78$\pm$0.31 & 16{,}154 & +6.4\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
\midrule
Predictor + compensation & 30\% & 129.94$\pm$0.75 & 15{,}761 & +9.1\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
Predictor + compensation & 50\% & 129.71$\pm$0.53 & 15{,}789 & +8.9\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The full KL-sparse pipeline adds 6.4\% overhead to dense inference (126.78 vs.\ 119.11\,ms/forward), of which the predictor's 32-layer forward pass contributes 3.17\,ms (2.7\%); the remainder arises from mask application and sparse FFN indexing.
Eliminating the compensation network saves an additional $\sim$2.7\% latency overhead and 67.2M parameters (the per-layer GEMV required for output rescaling); KL distillation thus provides both quality and efficiency advantages over BCE-based approaches.
The overhead is near-identical at 30\% and 50\% sparsity because the predictor runs the same computation regardless of target sparsity; only the top-$k$ threshold changes.

\section*{Limitations}

Our findings are bounded by three key limitations.
\textbf{Sparsity sweet spot.} 30\% appears to be the lowest-degradation level for downstream fidelity; at 40\%, MMLU drops to 35.5\% (vs.\ 40.7\% at 30\%), and at 50\%, all methods collapse to near-random on reasoning tasks. A separate predictor must be retrained per target.
\textbf{Knowledge-intensive regression.} KL consistently underperforms magnitude-based methods on MMLU and GSM8K across scales (8B: $-$5.2pp MMLU; 14B: $-$20pp GSM8K), suggesting distribution-matching objectives systematically sacrifice reasoning-critical pathways.
\textbf{Training data homogeneity.} All predictors are trained on WikiText-103 (English Wikipedia). OOD evaluation on C4 shows preserved KL advantage but $31\times$ higher cross-seed variance (CV=6.3\% vs.\ 0.2\% in-domain), indicating domain sensitivity. Batched inference, where sparsity patterns must be intersected across sequences, may reduce effective sparsity and is not evaluated. Evaluation is limited to 7--14B; scaling to 70B+ and wall-clock speedup via sparse kernels remain future work.

\section{Introduction}

How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
While MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} applies KL-based mask optimization, it targets static N:M weight sparsity; activation sparsity requires masks that generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\%).
A target-swap ablation suggests that KL-discovered mask targets carry most of the quality information at inference: BCE trained on KL-derived targets reproduces KL quality (max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp at 50\%, s42), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20. Cross-layer gradient coupling is not the primary driver of PPL-level quality, but contributes meaningfully to downstream task fidelity---a PPL--downstream dissociation quantified in \S\ref{sec:perlayer}.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30 at 28.5\%) with stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.

Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with robust commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$20pp, MMLU $-$2.8pp).
This paper is primarily an empirical study: we do not propose a new architecture or algorithm, but rather characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. The empirical finding---that output-distribution alignment is the critical design dimension for learned sparsity---is the paper's central contribution. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support; we do not address latency optimization (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item An output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, decomposed by a per-layer KL control into signal type (dominates PPL; upper bound) and coupling scope (10--47\% on downstream tasks, $K{=}4$-corrected), with task-dependent downstream structure (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
\item Exploratory cross-scale evidence at 7--14B confirming output-distribution losses outperform intermediate losses regardless of coupling scope (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\item A target-swap ablation suggests that KL's discovered mask targets drive inference-stage quality; cross-layer coupling refines downstream fidelity beyond what PPL captures (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
\item These mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:compensation}).
\end{itemize}

\caption{Method overview: a lightweight per-layer predictor produces importance scores trained via KL divergence with Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation. At inference, scores feed TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation without compensation networks.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure}

To isolate cross-layer coupling, we train per-layer KL predictors that mask $K$ random layers per step and compute KL on the full model output, preserving the output-distribution signal without cross-layer gradients.

At $K{=}1$, per-layer KL achieves 9.05$\pm$0.02, within 2.7\% of end-to-end KL (8.81$\pm$0.02), while per-layer MSE degrades to 18.52$\pm$1.68 ($2.05\times$ worse). For PPL, signal type\footnote{We use ``signal type'' as shorthand for the training objective's optimization target (output distribution vs.\ intermediate activations); this dimension also entails differences in gradient flow topology and optimization landscape that are not independently controlled.} accounts for the majority of the gap. This is an upper bound: the $K{=}1$ control conflates coupling removal with train--inference mismatch (training 1/32 layers; inference all 32); a $K{=}4$ control partially deconfounds this.

-The $K{=}1$ downstream gap conflates true coupling with train--inference mismatch (training masks 1/32 layers; inference applies all 32). A 3-seed $K{=}4$ control\footnote{Actual sparsity 29.6\%; per-layer sparsity std=0.003 (near-uniform).} decomposes this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:k4_downstream}): \emph{coupling-dominated}---ARC-c (97\% residual gap) and WG (67\%) indicate genuine cross-layer benefits for commonsense; \emph{mismatch-dominated}---PPL (67\% closure) and GSM8K (71\%)\footnote{GSM8K $K{=}4$: 7.0$\pm$1.6 (3-seed); high variance limits precision of gap closure estimate.} gaps largely close; \emph{anomalous}---MMLU exceeds E2E across all seeds (42.7$\pm$1.4 vs.\ 40.7$\pm$1.3), explained by $K{=}4$'s near-uniform allocation matching uniform inference (Appendix~\ref{app:constraint}). % exp_id: perlayer_kl_30_3seed, perlayer_kl_downstream, mse30_downstream_decomp, perlayer_kl_k4_3seed

-Output-distribution alignment is the dominant design dimension for PPL (signal type accounts for the majority of the gap; upper bound, confounded by train--inference mismatch in $K{=}1$); cross-layer coupling contributes 10--47\% on downstream tasks (3-seed $K{=}4$-corrected); MMLU anomalously favors $K{=}4$, reflecting allocation alignment (Appendices~\ref{app:k4_downstream},~\ref{app:constraint}).

-A predictor ($<$1\% of base) reduces TEAL's PPL by 14.5\% via masks 46--68\% divergent from magnitude; KL outperforms TEAL on commonsense but underperforms on knowledge tasks across tested scales---a learned allocation trade-off (Appendix~\ref{app:constraint}).
-Limitations include MMLU/GSM8K regression, absence of wall-clock speedup, and evaluation bounded at 7--14B.

The near-equivalence of KL and JSD suggests the divergence measure matters less than whether the loss optimizes through the output distribution; cross-layer scope provides additional downstream benefits (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}). % exp_id: bce30_uniform_s42, rkl30_downstream_3seed
\paragraph{Per-Layer KL: Decomposing Signal Type and Coupling Scope.}
\label{sec:perlayer}
To isolate cross-layer coupling, we train per-layer KL predictors that mask $K$ random layers per step and compute KL on the full model output, preserving the output-distribution signal without cross-layer gradients.
At $K{=}1$, per-layer KL achieves 9.05$\pm$0.02, within 2.7\% of end-to-end KL (8.81$\pm$0.02), while per-layer MSE degrades to 18.52$\pm$1.68 ($2.05\times$ worse). For PPL, signal type\footnote{We use ``signal type'' as shorthand for the training objective's optimization target (output distribution vs.\ intermediate activations); this dimension also entails differences in gradient flow topology and optimization landscape that are not independently controlled.} accounts for the majority of the gap. This is an upper bound: the $K{=}1$ control conflates coupling removal with train--inference mismatch (training 1/32 layers; inference all 32); a $K{=}4$ control partially deconfounds this.
The $K{=}1$ downstream gap conflates true coupling with train--inference mismatch (training masks 1/32 layers; inference applies all 32). A 3-seed $K{=}4$ control\footnote{Actual sparsity 29.6\%; per-layer sparsity std=0.003 (near-uniform).} decomposes this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:k4_downstream}): \emph{coupling-dominated}---ARC-c (97\% residual gap) and WG (67\%) indicate genuine cross-layer benefits for commonsense; \emph{mismatch-dominated}---PPL (67\% closure) and GSM8K (71\%) gaps largely close; \emph{anomalous}---MMLU exceeds E2E across all seeds (42.7$\pm$1.4 vs.\ 40.7$\pm$1.3), explained by $K{=}4$'s near-uniform allocation matching uniform inference (Appendix~\ref{app:constraint}). % exp_id: perlayer_kl_30_3seed, perlayer_kl_downstream, mse30_downstream_decomp, perlayer_kl_k4_3seed

Learned sparsity predictors for SwiGLU LLMs predominantly use binary cross-entropy (BCE), training each neuron independently, yet inference allocates budgets globally via top-$k$ ranking.
We train lightweight predictors ($<$1\% of base parameters) with forward KL divergence, coupling all mask decisions through the output distribution.
On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 30\% sparsity, the KL predictor reduces perplexity by 14.5\% over TEAL at matched sparsity, with commonsense gains but knowledge-intensive decline; post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) becomes redundant.
Output-distribution optimization yields masks that diverge 46--68\% from magnitude-based targets; a target-swap ablation suggests these discovered patterns carry most of the quality information: BCE trained on KL-derived targets approaches KL-level PPL (max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp, 3-seed).
Signal type (output-distribution vs.\ intermediate loss) accounts for the majority of the PPL gap at 30\% (upper bound; not fully orthogonal with coupling scope).
Cross-layer coupling contributes 10--47\% on downstream tasks (3-seed $K{=}4$-corrected; commonsense 22--47\%, reasoning 10\%).
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Qwen-2.5-14B confirms PPL generalization with scale-dependent downstream effects.
This is primarily an empirical study; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here.
